hints: Think about what happens to photosynthesis if you increase light, $CO_2$ and temperature one at a time - what if increasing one of them makes no difference?
Focus on the idea of being in shortest supply and holding back the rate while other factors are present in excess.
walkthrough:
Think About Several Inputs At Once**
Photosynthesis needs light, $CO_2$, water and a suitable temperature together. Imagine all are available except one is very low. That one will hold back the whole process, just like a narrow bottleneck holds back flow through a pipe.

Link Shortage To Rate**
A limiting factor is the single factor of several that is in shortest supply. Increasing it will increase the rate, but increasing any other factor will have no effect until a different factor becomes limiting.
Final answer: The factor present at its lowest value / in shortest supply; that prevents an increase in the rate of photosynthesis when other factors are not limiting.

hints: Think about what is living in the soil in the lower chamber besides the plant, and what gas all living cells release.
Consider how that extra gas would affect the carefully controlled $CO_2$ concentration around the leaves if the seal was not there.
walkthrough:
Spot The Hidden Source Of $CO_2$**
Soil contains roots plus bacteria, fungi and other microorganisms. All of these respire aerobically and release $CO_2$ into the soil air. That $CO_2$ is not part of the set concentration.

Protect The Leaf Chamber**
The investigation is testing exact atmospheric $CO_2$ concentrations around the leaves, such as 0.033% and 0.066%. A gas-tight seal stops unwanted $CO_2$ from soil and root respiration diffusing up and increasing the $CO_2$ around the leaves, which would make the results invalid.
Final answer: To prevent $CO_2$ from soil respiration entering the air around leaves; $CO_2$ from respiration of soil microorganisms and plant roots would alter the controlled $CO_2$ concentration.

hints: Look carefully at the shape of curve A in Fig. 2.1 - where does it rise steeply and where does it flatten to about 2.0 arbitrary units?
Recall what extra light provides for the light dependent reactions, and why that stops helping once another raw material runs out.
Identify the light intensity around 6-7 au as the turning point and name what takes over as limiting when light no longer does.
walkthrough:
Describe The Rising Section**
For set A at normal $CO_2$, from 0 to about 6 au light intensity the mean rate rises from 0 to about 1.9 arbitrary units. More light means more ATP and reduced NADP from the light dependent reactions, so more $CO_2$ can be fixed. Here light intensity is the main limiting factor.

Describe The Plateau Section**
Above about 6-7 au the curve for A flattens at about 2.0 arbitrary units up to 10 au. Increasing light further has no effect, so light is no longer limiting.

Explain The Switch In Limitation**
At high light, something else is now in shortest supply and holds the rate constant. With only normal $CO_2$ at 0.033%, $CO_2$ concentration (or temperature) becomes limiting for the Calvin cycle.

Final answer: At low light intensity up to 6-7 au, rate increases with light intensity as light is limiting; above 6-7 au rate levels off at ~2.0 au and remains constant as another factor, e.g. $CO_2$ concentration, is limiting.

hints: Compare the plateau values at high light - set B reaches about 3.6 while set A reaches about 2.0 - what is the only growing condition that differs?
Think about where $CO_2$ is used in photosynthesis and how extra $CO_2$ lets the plant make full use of abundant light and ATP.
walkthrough:
Link Extra $CO_2$ To Higher Rate**
At high light intensities, e.g. 8-10 au, light is plentiful for both sets but B photosynthesises much faster. B was grown and measured at double $CO_2$, so more $CO_2$ molecules are available to combine with RuBP catalysed by rubisco.

Explain Relief Of Limitation**
In set A, normal $CO_2$ limits the Calvin cycle even when ATP and reduced NADP are abundant. In set B, the higher $CO_2$ removes that limitation, allowing more triose phosphate production, so the plateau is much higher.

Final answer: Set B has double the $CO_2$ concentration (0.066% vs 0.033%); more $CO_2$ for fixation in the Calvin cycle / light independent reactions, so $CO_2$ is less limiting and higher rate is reached at high light.

hints: Note that both C and D are now tested across the same range of $CO_2$ in Fig. 2.2, yet D is higher at every $CO_2$ - so think long-term growth effect, not just immediate $CO_2$.
Think about what structures inside a leaf capture light and what enzyme fixes $CO_2$ - how could leaves grown in high $CO_2$ build more of these?
Consider how $CO_2$ gets into the leaf and how leaf thickness or diffusion distance could change with growth in high $CO_2$.
Put together 4 distinct structural or biochemical adaptations that let D use $CO_2$ more efficiently per unit area.
walkthrough:
Recognise Acclimatisation Not Just Immediate $CO_2$**
Fig. 2.2 tests both sets at the same $CO_2$ concentrations, yet D reaches about 4.8 while C reaches only about 3.0 at 6 au $CO_2$. This shows D plants, grown from seed at double $CO_2$, have developed to use $CO_2$ more effectively per unit leaf area.

More Light Harvesting And Fixation Machinery**
D leaves can develop more chloroplasts and chlorophyll per unit area to trap more light, and more rubisco enzyme and RuBP acceptor to fix $CO_2$ faster in the Calvin cycle. That raises the maximum capacity for photosynthesis.

Better $CO_2$ Supply To Cells**
D leaves can develop more stomata, allowing faster diffusion of $CO_2$ into air spaces, and thinner leaves which shorten the diffusion distance to mesophyll cells. Together with the extra enzymes, this explains the consistently higher curve for D.

Final answer: Plants in D adapted to high $CO_2$ during growth; have more chlorophyll / chloroplasts, more rubisco / RuBP, more stomata for $CO_2$ uptake, thinner leaves / shorter diffusion pathway, giving higher rate per unit area even at same test $CO_2$.
